I ran one random circuit on IQM's free Garnet test device (garnet:mock) with 1000 shots. Job ID 01a16044-478c-76ba-a451-8d02dc922ef3 finished with status DONE.

What I ran: I used 8 connected Garnet qubits: QB1, QB2, QB3, QB4, QB5, QB8, QB9 and QB10. The circuit has 10 cycles. In each cycle, every qubit gets a random half-turn-style gate (sqrt X, sqrt Y or sqrt W), and then a layer of CZ two-qubit gates acts on pairs of neighbouring qubits. That gives 10 layers of two-qubit gates and 28 CZ gates in total. After transpiling to Garnet's native gates, the circuit had 64 single-qubit gates, 28 CZ gates and a depth of 22. I also computed the exact output probabilities of the circuit on my laptop. That step took a fraction of a second.

The scores: xeb_measured is 0.066 and xeb_ideal is 0.882. A local check with 1000 samples drawn from the exact distribution scored 0.918, which is close to the ideal value as expected.

What the score means: Linear XEB asks one question. Do the measured bitstrings land on the outcomes that the circuit makes most likely? A score of 0 means the samples are no better than random guessing. A score near 1 (0.88 here) is what a perfect quantum computer would get. A real noisy chip scores somewhere in between. The score roughly equals the chance that the whole circuit ran without an error.

Why the measured score is near 0 here: garnet:mock is a free test endpoint. It does not simulate your circuit. It returns placeholder counts. Only 8 different bitstrings came back, such as 00000000 and 11111111. A real 8-qubit random circuit spreads its results over many of the 256 possible bitstrings. So the 0.066 shows that the scoring pipeline works and that the mock output does not match the circuit. It tells us nothing about Garnet's hardware quality. To get a real hardware score, the same circuit would have to run on real Garnet, which costs credits.

Why 8 qubits is easy and 50 is not: To score XEB, or to fake the samples, a normal computer has to track one number for every possible bitstring. For 8 qubits that is 2^8 = 256 numbers, which any laptop handles instantly. Each added qubit doubles the count. At 50 qubits there are about 10^15 numbers, and storing them takes about 16 petabytes of memory. At 53 qubits or more, with enough layers, the best known classical methods need supercomputer-scale time or memory. That is the size where Google (2019) and later groups claimed a quantum advantage for random circuit sampling. The principle is that the work for a classical simulation grows exponentially with the number of qubits. A quantum chip just runs the circuit. There is one catch. At that size nobody can compute the ideal probabilities directly any more, so the score itself has to be estimated from smaller or simpler versions of the circuit.
